title: Job quality: Employment growth conceals unequal progression
desc: Argues that procurement, funding, wage policy and skills reform can improve work quality, though many benefits remain prospective.

kps.k: Employment growth can conceal insecurity, unequal pay and weak career progression.
kps.d: The Hourglass Economy argues that London’s post-2008 recovery should be judged by job quality, not employment totals alone. It attributes resilient employment partly to reduced hours, casualisation and frozen pay, and reports the UK’s highest regional pay inequality. Its evidence combines labour-market findings with first-hand accounts. This concerns London’s wider labour market, not law-firm staffing or AI-driven displacement.

qs.q: Despite growing wealth and employment, London is a highly polarised city  and suffers the greatest level of pay inequality of any region in the UK.1 The  reality is that for those who work on low-pay or with insecure contracts, have  dependent children at home, or left school with few qualifications, living and  working in London can be an everyday struggle.
qs.a: The Hourglass Economy: An analysis of London's labour market · Regulators & courts · 2016

qs.q: Following the 2008 global financial services  crash, employment in London – and across the rest of the country – remained  buoyant, with businesses responding to the downturn by reducing hours,  introducing greater casualisation, and freezing pay in order to protect jobs.
qs.a: The Hourglass Economy: An analysis of London's labour market · Regulators & courts · 2016

kps.k: The central disagreement concerns what counts as labour-market success.
kps.d: The report contrasts the Chief Economic Advisor’s favourable assessment of a 72.5% employment rate—the highest recorded since 1992—with its own findings of less sustainable employment, elusive progression and underused skills. It calls for routine job-quality measures and for London Living Wage monitoring to count workers benefiting, rather than simply participating employers. The disagreement concerns the adequacy of headline indicators, rather than a challenge to the reported employment rate.

kps.k: Public leadership, funding and procurement offer practical ways to improve job quality despite limited statutory powers.
kps.d: The report credits mayoral apprenticeship promotion and doubled SME apprenticeship grants, but criticises reluctance to require Living Wage accreditation from recipients of GLA or TfL capital funding. It recommends employer–union collaboration, particularly in retail and hospitality, to improve contracts and pay while recognising employers’ needs and ability to pay. It also proposes transparent job advertisements and public-sector leadership on flexible hiring, extending these practices through partnerships and procurement.

kps.k: Wider Living Wage adoption is a policy objective; a legal mandate requires assessment of employment effects.
kps.d: To address in-work poverty, the report advocates broader voluntary adoption and accreditation-linked business-rate discounts. Its proposal to consider mandating the London Living Wage by 2020 was a historical feasibility recommendation, not an enacted policy or an unconditional demand. It calls for analysis of potential job creation and losses, using the OBR’s 2015 national analysis as a model.

qs.q: Recommendation 4  The incoming Mayor, and the LEP, should seek ways to further the positive  impact of the London Living Wage, and reduce the proportion of Londoners  facing in-work poverty.

kps.k: Skills reform and devolution aim to create routes into better work, but their benefits remain prospective.
kps.d: The report cites the Mayor’s acknowledged shortfall against a target of 250,000 apprenticeship starts by April 2016 and the finding that 61% of starts during his second term were intermediate-level courses. It treats these as shortcomings in scale and quality, while welcoming existing initiatives. It proposes industry-tailored training, careers advancement support for low-paid workers, and devolved post-16 funding and responsibility. A pooled London employment-support budget and local investment in innovation would, it predicts, improve targeted support and expand mid- and high-skilled jobs; the supplied material does not demonstrate those outcomes.

vlens.an: The selected source in this professional voice directly supports the proposition that employment growth can coexist with poor job quality. It treats pay inequality, insecure contracts and weak progression as reasons not to equate a high employment rate with labour-market success. It also supports active public intervention through procurement, wage policy, skills provision and devolution. Material variation lies in evidential status and policy strength: the diagnosis of unequal job quality is presented as a finding, whereas many claimed benefits of devolved investment and reform are predictions rather than demonstrated outcomes; similarly, a Living Wage mandate is proposed for feasibility assessment rather than endorsed unconditionally. Because this facet contains one curated source, its position should not be generalized to regulators, courts and professional bodies as a whole.

elens.an: The source supports the proposition that employment growth can conceal poor job quality and unequal progression. It contrasts strong headline employment with evidence of insecure contracts, pay inequality, reduced hours, frozen pay, weak career progression and underused skills, and therefore argues that labour-market success should include quality measures rather than employment totals alone. It also supports the proposition’s proposed policy mechanisms—procurement, public funding, Living Wage policy, flexible hiring, industry-tailored training and devolved skills and employment support. Material internal variation lies in evidential status and policy caution: the diagnosis of existing labour-market problems is presented as a finding, whereas many claimed benefits of devolution and skills reform are prospective. Likewise, the report advocates wider Living Wage adoption but recommends assessing the employment effects before any mandate. This assessment concerns the single supplied source and should not be read as representative of all sources from 2015–2022 or of wider opinion on automation; indeed, the source addresses London’s general labour market rather than AI-driven displacement.
